name: Finetune.Lora
comment:
LoRA (low-rank adaptation) adapts a dense layer by training a small update beside its weight
rather than the weight itself. This module is the _adapter_ that makes that update: its parameters,
their description, and the functions that apply it or fold it into a weight.

The layer's weight W has shape (i, o), from `i` input features to `o` output features, as in
`Nn.Linear`. The adapter holds two factors, A of shape (i, r) and B of shape (r, o), and the update
it makes to W is (alpha / rank) · A · B. The product A · B has W's shape but a matrix rank of at
most r, and it is described by r · (i + o) numbers instead of i · o. The _rank_ is a number in the
adapter's record, which `params` sets to the size r, and _alpha_ is a constant chosen with the
adapter; the factor alpha / rank scales the product. Both are plain numbers in the adapter's record,
not tensors, so neither is trained.

`params` describes the adapter alone, with A and B both trainable. A's first values are drawn from a
normal distribution and B's are zero, so the product A · B is zero at first unless one of A's first
values is not finite, and training moves it from there. The base layer is not part of that
description. It has its own, such as `Nn.Linear.params`, whose fields are trainable unless the
description is passed to `Param.frozen`.

Besides `delta` itself, this module offers two ways to use the adapter. `apply` computes the base
layer's output and adds the update's contribution to it, without forming the (i, o) update. `merge`
adds the update to a weight, which can then serve as an ordinary `Linear`'s weight, and `unmerge`
takes it out again. The two ways agree mathematically but compute in different orders, so their
results can differ by rounding.

aliases.name: Lora
aliases.comment:
A low-rank adapter for an (i, o) weight in dtype `d`: the factors A (`a`) and B (`b`) and the
two numbers that scale their product by alpha / rank.

`params` sets `rank` to the size of `r`. A record made any other way can hold any `Int` there.
`Param.sig` of a `params` description compares the field with the description's value, as
`Param.config` describes, but nothing compares it with the shapes of `a` and `b`, and the scale is
computed from this field, not from the shapes.
aliases.type: { a : Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 i r), b : Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 r o), alpha : Basics.Float, rank : Basics.Int }

values.name: apply
values.comment:
Returns `base` applied to the `n` rows of `x`, as `Nn.Linear.apply` computes it (x · weight +
bias), plus the adapter's contribution (alpha / rank) · x · A · B.

`x` is multiplied by A first, so the contribution goes through an (n, r) intermediate and the
(i, o) update is never formed. Applying `merge p base.weight` with the same bias gives the same
result mathematically, but can differ from this one by rounding.
values.type: Nn.Linear.Linear d i o -> Finetune.Lora.Lora d i r o -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n i) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n o)

values.name: delta
values.comment:
Returns the adapter's update to an (i, o) weight, (alpha / rank) · A · B, with the scale
taken from `p.alpha` and `p.rank`.
values.type: Finetune.Lora.Lora d i r o -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 i o)

values.name: merge
values.comment: Returns the weight `w` with the adapter's update, `delta p`, added.
values.type: Finetune.Lora.Lora d i r o -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 i o) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 i o)

values.name: params
values.comment:
Returns the description of an adapter for an (i, o) weight in dtype `dt`, with the given `rank`,
`alpha` and `initStd`.

`a` and `b` are trainable fields, in that order. `a`'s first values are drawn as `Param.normal`
describes, with standard deviation `initStd`, and `b`'s are all 0. `alpha` and `rank` are config
fields holding the given `alpha` and the size of the given `rank`: they have no buffers, and every
record the description builds holds those values.
values.type: Tensor.DType Basics.Float d -> { rank : Tensor.Dim r, alpha : Basics.Float, initStd : Basics.Float } -> Tensor.Dim i -> Tensor.Dim o -> Param.Spec (Finetune.Lora.Lora d i r o)

values.name: unmerge
values.comment:
Returns the weight `w` with the adapter's update, `delta p`, subtracted. Given the adapter that
`merge` added, this recovers the original weight up to rounding wherever the merged weight `w` is
finite.
values.type: Finetune.Lora.Lora d i r o -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 i o) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 i o)

name: Finetune.Qlora
comment:
QLoRA (Dettmers et al. 2023) fine-tunes a dense layer whose weight is frozen and kept in a
compact form, each element replaced by a small integer code, while only a LoRA adapter beside it
(`Finetune.Lora`) is trained. This module is that frozen weight: how a parameter description holds
it, how its codes are computed from a weight in Elm, and how a graph turns them back into a dense
weight and applies it with an adapter.

The weight W has shape (i, o), from `i` input features to `o` output features, as in `Nn.Linear`.
To _quantize_ it, its elements are taken in row-major order and cut into _blocks_ of consecutive
elements, as many in each as the _block size_ (`Quantized`'s `blockSize`). Each block has a _scale_
and each element is replaced by its _code_. When the elements are all finite, a block's scale is the
largest magnitude among its elements, or 1 when they are all 0, and an element's code is the index
of the value in the _codebook_ nearest to the element divided by its block's scale. To _dequantize_
it, each element is its code's codebook value times its block's scale.

The codebook is _NF4_ (4-bit NormalFloat), the 16 values of `codebook`. A code is therefore in
0 … 15 and needs only 4 bits, but here each code is stored in a byte of its own, as a `u8`.

The codes and scales are data fields of the description (`Param.data`): training does not update
them, and `Param.initial` and `Train.initial` give them zeros. `quantize` computes their contents,
as bytes for `Train.initialFrom` or for a runtime that takes buffers as bytes.

Two of the ways `quantize`'s bytes can disagree with the description are these. `quantize` always
writes the scales as f32, whatever dtype the description gives them. And `blockSize` should divide
i × o, which nothing checks: when it does not, `blocks` leaves out the shorter last block that
`quantize` gives, and `dequantize` takes the blocks' length from the number of scales, not from
`blockSize`. `Train.initialFrom` checks only the bytes' lengths. For a non-empty weight
given to `quantize` and `params` with the same positive block size and dimensions, it refuses
`quantize`'s bytes in either case, with one exception: float64 scales with i × o strictly between
the block size and twice it. The lengths then agree, and two f32 scales are read as one f64 scale.

unions.name: Block
unions.comment:
The tag of the axis that indexes a weight's blocks, the one axis of `Quantized`'s `scales`.

Its constructor is not exposed, so outside this package a `Dim Block` is made only by `blocks`.

aliases.name: Quantized
aliases.comment:
A frozen (i, o) weight in quantized form, whose dequantized elements have dtype `d`.

`codes` holds each element's code, an index into `codebook`, not its value. `scales` holds one
scale per block, in block order. `blockSize` is the `size` given to `params`; `dequantize` does not
read it, and takes the blocks' length from the number of scales instead.
aliases.type: { codes : Tensor.Tensor Basics.Int Tensor.U8 (Tensor.R2 i o), scales : Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R1 Finetune.Qlora.Block), blockSize : Basics.Int }

values.name: apply
values.comment:
Returns the `n` rows of `x` multiplied by the dequantized weight, plus the adapter's
contribution: x · `dequantize q` + x · `Lora.delta lora`. No bias is added.

Unlike `Lora.apply`, this forms the adapter's whole (i, o) update with `Lora.delta` before
multiplying, rather than multiplying `x` by A and then by B.
values.type: Finetune.Qlora.Quantized d i o -> Finetune.Lora.Lora d i r o -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n i) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n o)

values.name: blocks
values.comment:
Returns the dimension of the scales of an (i, o) weight cut into blocks of `size` elements:
i × o divided by `size` with Elm's `//`. A `size` of 0 or less is taken as 1.

Nothing checks that `size` divides i × o. When it does not, the partial last block that `quantize`
makes is not counted.
values.type: Basics.Int -> Tensor.Dim i -> Tensor.Dim o -> Tensor.Dim Finetune.Qlora.Block

values.name: codebook
values.comment:
The 16 NF4 values in ascending order, which a code indexes. They run from −1 to 1, are closer
together near 0 than near ±1, and include 0 itself.
values.type: List.List Basics.Float

values.name: dequantize
values.comment:
Returns the dense weight that `q` stands for: each element its code's `codebook` value times its
block's scale.

The blocks come from the number of scales, not from `q.blockSize`: with b scales, each block is the
next (i × o) / b elements in row-major order, and when b does not divide i × o the result is a
build error. The products are computed in f32 and then cast to the scales' dtype. A code of 16 or
more is an index outside `codebook`, which, like any index, is not checked when the graph is built;
`Tensor.Eval` refuses it when it runs the graph.
values.type: Finetune.Qlora.Quantized d i o -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 i o)

values.name: params
values.comment:
Returns the description of an (i, o) weight quantized in blocks of `size` elements, whose
scales have dtype `dt`.

`codes` and `scales`, in that order, are data fields, and `scales` has `blocks size i o` elements.
`blockSize` is a config field holding `size`. Since `quantize` writes f32 scales, the scales it
gives for a non-empty weight fit this description only when `dt` is `float32`.
values.type: Tensor.DType Basics.Float d -> Basics.Int -> Tensor.Dim i -> Tensor.Dim o -> Param.Spec (Finetune.Qlora.Quantized d i o)

values.name: quantize
values.comment:
Returns the codes and scales of a weight given as its elements in row-major order, as bytes in
the package encoding that `Train` describes: one byte per code, and one f32 per scale whatever
dtype the description gives the scales.

The elements are cut into blocks of `size` in list order, the last block holding whatever remains.
When the elements are all finite, a block's scale is the largest magnitude among its elements, or 1
when they are all 0, and an element's code is the index of the `codebook` value nearest to the
element divided by its block's scale, the lower index on a tie.

The two `Dim` arguments are not read, so the number of elements is not compared with i × o. With a
`size` of 0 or less and a non-empty list, cutting the list into blocks recurses without end, so
this gives no result (under JavaScript, the stack overflows).

The bytes are meant for `Train.initialFrom`, under the resident names `Param.names` gives the
description's `codes` and `scales` fields, or for a runtime that takes buffers as bytes.
`Train.initialFrom` checks only their length. Given the same `size`, i and o as `params`, that
refuses a wrong number of elements and, when the description's scales are f32, a positive `size`
that does not divide i × o. `Tensor.Eval` takes buffers as values, not bytes.
values.type: Basics.Int -> Tensor.Dim i -> Tensor.Dim o -> List.List Basics.Float -> { codes : Bytes.Bytes, scales : Bytes.Bytes }

name: Graph
comment:
Before a computation written with tensors can be run as a graph, it has to be fixed: which
tensors it is given, which it gives back, what each of them is called, and whether it is well
formed. This module does that. `build` turns a function from tensors to tensors into a `Graph`, the
value that both ways of running a graph take: `Tensor.Eval` runs a graph in plain Elm, and
`Graph.Max` writes it out for MAX.

    Graph.build "step" (Sig.pair inputsA inputsB) outputsSig (\( a, b ) -> ...)

The inputs and outputs are described by signatures (`Signature`), each of which matches a
structured Elm value to an ordered list of tensors. `build` makes one input tensor for each slot of
the input signature, builds the function's argument from them, applies the function, and lists the
tensors of its result with the output signature. Each input and output then gets a _spec_: a name,
a dtype, a shape and a _role_, which says how it is passed between the graph and whatever runs it
(see `Role`). The names come from the slots' labels, as `Signature.label` describes. A slot that has
not been given a label carries `arg`, which stays `arg` in the input signature and becomes `result`
in the output signature. A label that several slots carry is then numbered across the whole
signature (`x0`, `x1` ..), so several unlabelled inputs are named `arg0`, `arg1` and so on, and
several unlabelled outputs, or an unlabelled output and one labelled `result`, are named `result0`,
`result1` and so on. The numbers are not checked against the other names, so the labels `w`, `w`,
`w1` give the names `w0`, `w1`, `w1`.

A tensor made from operands that do not fit carries a _build error_, as `Tensor` describes. `build`
returns either a `Graph` or the list of what it found wrong, which can include build errors, each
message starting with the graph's name. Some failures come only later. For example, `Graph.Max`
refuses some operations on a GPU, and `Tensor.Eval` refuses some index values when it runs the
graph, as `Tensor` describes.

Building a graph also translates it into the operations MAX reads, so that `Graph.Max` has only to
place them on a device and write them.

unions.name: Role
unions.comment:
How a graph's input or output is passed between the graph and whatever runs it.

A `Fed` input is given with every run, and a `Fed` output is handed back from every run.

`Resident` carries a _resident name_: the name of a buffer that whatever runs the graph keeps from
one run to the next, such as a model's parameters. An input with that role reads the buffer, and an
output with the same resident name replaces its contents after the run. The graph only records the
role; keeping the buffer is up to whatever runs it. `Tensor.Eval` takes and returns a resident
input or output under its resident name, and any other under its spec's name.

Every slot `Signature` makes is `Fed`. Resident roles come from the signatures that `Param`,
`Train` and `Infer` build.

aliases.name: Graph
aliases.comment:
A computation that `build` accepted, with its inputs and outputs named and described: what
`Tensor.Eval` runs and what `Graph.Max` writes.

The only way to make one is `build`, or `function`, which calls it. Holding a `Graph` therefore
means that every check `build` makes has passed. What `build` does not check can still fail when
the graph is written for a device or run.

`==` and `Debug.toString` on a graph can go through the whole computation and visit a part once
for every use of it, which can take time exponential in the computation's depth. Comparing the bytes
`Graph.Max.toBytecode` writes for two graphs is far cheaper, but those bytes do not record the
roles of the inputs and outputs.

aliases.name: Spec
aliases.comment:
The description of one input or output of a graph: its name, its dtype, its shape and its role.

`dtype` is MAX's name for the element type: `"f16"`, `"bf16"`, `"f32"`, `"f64"`, `"si8"`, `"si32"`,
`"si64"`, `"ui8"`, `"ui64"` or `"bool"`, not the `I64` or `U8` of the dtype tags. `shape` lists the
size of each axis.
aliases.type: { name : String.String, dtype : String.String, shape : List.List Basics.Int, role : Graph.Role }

values.name: build
values.type: String.String -> Signature.Sig a -> Signature.Sig b -> (a -> b) -> Result.Result (List.List String.String) Graph.Graph

values.name: function
values.comment:
Builds, as `build` does, a graph whose one output is `body`'s result, named `result`. The
output's dtype and shape are those of the result.
values.type: String.String -> Signature.Sig a -> (a -> Tensor.Tensor k d s) -> Result.Result (List.List String.String) Graph.Graph

values.name: inputs
values.comment:
Returns the specs of the graph's inputs, in the order of the input signature's slots. The names
are made from the slots' labels, as the module docstring describes. A slot that has not been given
a label carries `arg`, so several such slots are named `arg0`, `arg1` and so on.
values.type: Graph.Graph -> List.List Graph.Spec

values.name: name
values.comment: Returns the name the graph was built with.
values.type: Graph.Graph -> String.String

values.name: outputs
values.comment:
Returns the specs of the graph's outputs, in the order of the output signature's slots. The
names are made from the slots' labels, as the module docstring describes. A slot that has not been
given a label carries `arg`, which becomes `result`, so several such slots, or one such slot and one
labelled `result`, are named `result0`, `result1` and so on.
values.type: Graph.Graph -> List.List Graph.Spec

name: Graph.Max
comment:
Modular MAX takes a graph as an MLIR module, and this module writes a built `Graph` as one: as
MLIR bytecode, the binary form MAX's graph compiler loads, or as MLIR's generic op text, the same
module written out to be read. How the bytes reach MAX, and how MAX runs them, is up to the
caller.

_MLIR_ is a compiler framework in which a program is a tree of operations, each named after the
_dialect_ it belongs to, as `mo.graph` belongs to `mo`. `Graph.build` has already checked the graph
and translated it into the operations of MAX's graph dialects, `mo` and `rmo`, so what is left here
is to place those operations on a device and write them. The bytecode is version 6 of MLIR's
bytecode format, which this package assumes is the version the MLIR inside MAX 26.7.0 reads.

_Placing_ the operations for a GPU writes into them where their tensors live; placing them for the
CPU adds nothing to them. Placing for the CPU cannot fail, so `toBytecode` and `toGenericText`
write for the CPU and return no `Result`. Placing for a GPU can: some operations are not written
for a GPU, and the graph is then refused with one message for each such operation. They are a
top-k along any axis but the last (from `Tensor.topK`, `bottomK` or `sort`), and every `cond` and
every `whileLoop` (`Tensor.Control`), wherever in the graph they appear.

What is written depends on the graph and the device alone, so writing one graph twice gives the
same bytes. The bytes hold the graph's name and the names, dtypes and shapes of its inputs and
outputs, but not their roles (`Graph.Role`).

Among what can be written with operands that name the wrong values, with nothing reporting it, are
operations inside the branches of a `cond` that depends on the arguments of the `cond` branch it is
written in, through its predicate, its arguments or a tensor its branches read; operations inside
the branches of a `cond` in a `whileLoop`'s test or step; and an operation that reads a value
computed two or more branches or loops out.

@docs toBytecode, toGenericText

unions.name: Device
unions.comment:
The device a graph is written for: the CPU, or, as `Gpu n`, the GPU with index `n`.

The index is written into the graph as given. Nothing here checks that the GPU exists or that `n`
is not negative.

values.name: toBytecode
values.comment:
Writes the graph as MLIR bytecode, placed for the CPU.

Two graphs that differ only in the roles of their inputs or outputs write the same bytes.
values.type: Graph.Graph -> Bytes.Bytes

values.name: toBytecodeOn
values.comment:
Writes the graph as MLIR bytecode, placed for the given device, or returns why it cannot be
placed there.

For `Gpu n`, the graph's inputs and the tensors its operations compute, constants included, are
placed on GPU `n`, except values such as shapes and axes that other operations read as operands,
which stay on the CPU. The result is `Err` when the graph holds a top-k along any axis but the last
(from `Tensor.topK`, `bottomK` or `sort`), a `cond` or a `whileLoop`, anywhere in it, with one
message for each MLIR operation refused, naming it.

`toBytecodeOn Cpu g` is always `Ok (toBytecode g)`.
values.type: Graph.Max.Device -> Graph.Graph -> Result.Result (List.List String.String) Bytes.Bytes

values.name: toGenericText
values.comment:
Writes the module `toBytecode` writes as MLIR's generic op text: each operation with its quoted
name, its operands, its regions, its attributes and its types, the one text form MLIR reads for an
operation of any dialect.
values.type: Graph.Graph -> String.String

values.name: toGenericTextOn
values.comment:
Writes the graph, placed for the given device, as MLIR's generic op text (see `toGenericText`),
or returns the refusals `toBytecodeOn` returns.
values.type: Graph.Max.Device -> Graph.Graph -> Result.Result (List.List String.String) String.String

name: Infer
comment:
A model that is run again and again, such as one producing text a token at a time, reads the
same parameters on every run and carries a _state_ from one run to the next, such as key/value
caches or diffusion latents. Sending the parameters and the state with every run, and receiving the
state back, would move them for nothing. This module builds graphs that leave both where the graph
runs.

It does so with resident roles (see `Graph.Role`): an input with a resident name reads a buffer that
whatever runs the graph keeps between runs, and an output with the same resident name replaces that
buffer's contents after the run. A graph made by `step` reads the parameters and the state as
resident inputs, and takes the rest of its input as fed inputs, given with each run. It gives back
the new state as resident outputs under the state's own names, so the new state takes the old one's
place, and gives the rest of its output back as fed outputs. The graph has no output for the
parameters, but nothing keeps a state's resident name from being a parameter's, and then the new
state replaces that parameter's buffer. A graph made by `initGraph` has no inputs and writes given
contents into the state's buffers.

The new state's tensors are matched to the state slots in order, and one without the dtype and
shape its slot declares is a build error. Every slot of the state signature and of the input
signature must declare a dtype and a shape, so `Signature.anyTensor` cannot be used there.

The parameters are resident under the names `Param.names` gives. Each state tensor is resident under
a name made from its slot's label: the labels of the state signature are numbered as `Graph`
describes, with `state` for a slot that has no label, and each is prefixed `infer.`. Numbering does
not always give distinct names (the labels `w`, `w`, `w1` give `infer.w0`, `infer.w1` and
`infer.w1`), and two state tensors with one name share one buffer. `step` and `initGraph` give one
state signature the same names.

A fed input whose slot declares the shape `[]` is declared with the shape `[1]`, and the function
given to `step` receives it reshaped to `[]`. The package assumes that MAX's C API takes no rank-0
inputs. Whatever runs the graph therefore gives such an input with the shape `[1]`. Parameter, state
and output slots are not widened in this way.

In this example, `Model.params` and `Model.step` stand for the user's own model, and the state is
two key/value caches (`Nn.KvCache`), whose slots are labelled `keys` and `values`. The state is
resident under `infer.keys0`, `infer.values0`, `infer.keys1` and `infer.values1`, and the rank-0
position is fed as `[1]`.

    decode =
        Infer.step "decode"
            Model.params
            (Sig.list 2 (KvCache.sig T.float32 kvHeads context headDim))
            (Sig.pair (Sig.i64 (T.r1 one)) (Sig.i64 T.scalar))
            (Sig.f32 (T.r2 one vocab))
            (\p caches ( token, position ) -> Model.step p caches token position)


# Graphs

@docs step, initGraph

values.name: initGraph
values.comment:
Builds the graph `graphName`, which has no inputs and whose outputs are the tensors of `value`,
resident under the names `step` gives the state `Sig state` describes; or returns what it found
wrong. Running it fills, where the graph runs, the buffers from which a graph made by `step` with
the same state signature reads its state.

The graph has no inputs, so a tensor of `value` that reads another graph's input is refused, as
`Graph.build` describes.

The tensors of `value` are checked against the state slots as `step` checks a new state: each must
have its slot's dtype and shape, with the same caveats, and any past the last slot are dropped. A
state slot that declares no dtype or no shape is refused before the graph is built.
values.type: String.String -> Signature.Sig state -> state -> Result.Result (List.List String.String) Graph.Graph

values.name: step
values.comment:
Builds the graph `graphName`, which applies `f` to the parameters the spec describes, the state
`Sig state` describes and the input `Sig input` describes, and gives back `f`'s new state and its
output as `Sig output` lists it; or returns what it found wrong.

The graph's inputs are, in order: one resident input for each tensor field of the spec, under its
name from `Param.names`; one resident input for each state slot, under the names the module
docstring describes; and one fed input for each input slot, a slot declaring `[]` being declared
`[1]` and reshaped to `[]` before `f` receives it. Its outputs are the new state's tensors, up to
one per state slot, followed by the output's tensors, given in that order to the state slots,
resident under the state's names, and then to the output's slots, which are fed. The parameters
are not outputs.

Each tensor of the new state must have the dtype and shape of its state slot; one that differs is a
build error naming the state and both dtypes and shapes. That check does not look for an earlier
build error. A new state tensor that carries a build error, or is built on one, may have a guessed
dtype and shape; when they differ from its slot's it gets this error as well, and when the earlier
error was the tensor's own, this error replaces it. The new state's tensors are matched to the state
slots in order, and any past the last slot are dropped without an error. A new state with too few
tensors is not refused when the output has as many tensors more than its slots: the output's first
tensors then take the remaining state slots, resident under the state's names and without this
check.

A state or input slot that declares no dtype or no shape is refused before the graph is built, with
errors that name the slot's position and do not begin with the graph's name. Otherwise the graph is
built by `Graph.build`, and its errors are returned. `Graph.build`'s round-trip check covers the
parameter spec, `Sig state` and `Sig input` on the graph's inputs, but not `Sig output`, nor
`Sig state` on the new state. Its count of output tensors covers the new state and the output
together.
values.type: String.String -> Param.Spec r -> Signature.Sig state -> Signature.Sig input -> Signature.Sig output -> (r -> state -> input -> ( state, output )) -> Result.Result (List.List String.String) Graph.Graph

name: Nn
comment:
The parts of a neural network that hold no parameters of their own: losses, dropout, attention,
pooling and upsampling, timestep embeddings, and two helpers that build an attention mask and
repeat attention heads. Each returns a tensor or a mask whose element values, like those of the
operations of `Tensor`, are computed only when it is run.

Like those of `Tensor`, the functions here that transform a tensor take it last, so that
`logits |> crossEntropy targets` and `queries |> attention options keys values` read left to right.
`causalMaskAt` takes its position tensor first.

The types fix ranks and axis tags but not sizes, so some sizes are checked when a result is made,
and a mismatch is a build error, as `Tensor` describes: a pooling window that does not divide the
image, a declared result size that differs from the computed one, an odd embedding width, a head
count asked of `repeatHeads` that is not a multiple of its input's. In the attention functions
these axes of size 1 are repeated to match a larger size, not refused: a head count of 1 in the
queries, keys or values, an axis of a mask or bias, and, in `causalAttention`, a single query,
which then attends to every key. Element values are not checked: a class label outside its range,
or a `causalMaskAt` position beyond the last key, is used as given.

Images are NHWC: rank-4 tensors of (batch, height, width, channels). Attention works on rank-3
tensors of (heads, positions, features) and treats each head separately. In the attention
functions' types `h` is the number of heads, `s` the number of query positions, `t` the number of
key positions, `j` the features of a query or key and `e` the features of a value. A mask says
which keys a query may read: True where it may, False where it may not.

# Masks and heads

A key/value cache holds the keys and values of the positions already processed, so that queries at
new positions can attend to them without computing them again. In grouped-query attention there are
fewer key/value heads, `g`, than query heads, `h`, and each key/value head serves a group of query
heads.

values.name: attention
values.comment:
Returns scaled dot-product attention, each head separately: for each query, a weighted sum of
the values, the weights coming from the query's scores against the keys.

In each head the scores are the dot products of the `s` queries with the `t` keys, divided by √j,
plus `bias` when it is given, and a softmax over each query's `t` scores makes them weights. `mask`
and `bias` are shared by every head, and either is also repeated along an axis where it has size 1;
one with a broadcast axis is a build error.

Where `mask` is False the score is replaced by −10⁹, or by −65504, the lowest finite value, for
`f16`, not by −∞: a query whose keys are all masked gives every key the same weight. For `f16` and
`bf16` the softmax is computed in `f32` and its result cast back.
values.type: { mask : Maybe.Maybe (Tensor.Mask (Tensor.R2 s t)), bias : Maybe.Maybe (Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s t)) } -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R3 h t j) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R3 h t e) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R3 h s j) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R3 h s e)

values.name: avgPool2d
values.comment:
Returns the mean of each `k` × `k` window of the image `x`, with the windows and the checks of
`maxPool2d`.
values.type: Basics.Int -> Tensor.Dim h2 -> Tensor.Dim w2 -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h w c) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h2 w2 c)

values.name: causalAttention
values.comment:
Returns `attention` with no bias and a causal mask: query i attends to keys 0 … i. The mask is
`s` × `s`, `s` being the number of queries, so with more than one query a number of keys other than
`s` is a build error, and a single query attends to every key, however many there are.
values.type: Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R3 h s j) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R3 h s e) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R3 h s j) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R3 h s e)

values.name: causalMaskAt
values.comment:
Returns the causal mask for `s` new queries over a key/value cache of `t` positions, the first
new query being at position `p`: query i, at position `p` + i, may attend to keys 0 … `p` + i.

`p` is a tensor, so it can be a graph input, and nothing checks it against `t`.
values.type: Tensor.Tensor Basics.Int Tensor.I64 Tensor.R0 -> Tensor.Dim s -> Tensor.Dim t -> Tensor.Mask (Tensor.R2 s t)

values.name: crossEntropy
values.comment:
Returns the softmax cross-entropy of `logits` against `targets`, averaged over the `n` rows: the
mean over rows of −Σ targets · log (softmax logits), the softmax taken along each row.

`targets` need not be one-hot; any rows of weights are accepted. The gradient with respect to
`logits` is taken to be (softmax logits − targets) / n, which is the derivative of the loss only
where every row of `targets` sums to 1.
values.type: Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n c) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n c) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d Tensor.R0

values.name: crossEntropyIndices
values.comment:
Returns `crossEntropy` of `logits` against the one-hot rows of `labels`: row i is 1 at the class
`labels[i]` and 0 elsewhere.

A label outside 0 … c − 1 gives a row of zeros, with no error when the tensor is made or run. That
row adds 0 to the sum but still counts in the n rows the sum is averaged over, and the gradient
still passes softmax / n back to that row's logits.
values.type: Tensor.Tensor Basics.Int i (Tensor.R1 n) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n c) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d Tensor.R0

values.name: dropout
values.comment:
Returns `x` with some elements dropped: for a `rate` between 0 and 1, each element is set to 0
with probability `rate`, and the others are multiplied by 1 / (1 − `rate`), which keeps each
element's expected value. When `training` is False, or `rate` is 0 or less, `x` is returned
unchanged. A `rate` of 1 or more drops every element, and at exactly 1 the gradient with respect
to `x` is NaN, since the factor 1 / (1 − `rate`) is then infinite and multiplies a zero cotangent.

Which elements are dropped is a draw on `seed`, as `Tensor.Random` describes, so two calls with one
seed, one rate and tensors of one shape drop the same elements; `Tensor.Random.salt` gives each
call its own seed. A broadcast axis of `x` becomes a real axis of size 1 in the result, as with
`Tensor.zerosLike`, unless `x` is returned unchanged.
values.type: { rate : Basics.Float, training : Basics.Bool } -> Tensor.Random.Seed -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d s -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d s

values.name: maxPool2d
values.comment:
Returns the maximum of each `k` × `k` window of the image `x`, the windows not overlapping: the
stride is `k`. `h2` and `w2` are the result's height and width, h / k and w / k. A `k` of 0 or
less, or one that does not divide both `h` and `w`, is a build error, and so is an `h2` or `w2`
other than the computed size.
values.type: Basics.Int -> Tensor.Dim h2 -> Tensor.Dim w2 -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h w c) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h2 w2 c)

values.name: mseLoss
values.comment:
Returns the mean, over every element, of the squared difference between `predictions` and
`targets`.
values.type: Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d s -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d s -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d Tensor.R0

values.name: repeatHeads
values.comment:
Returns the `g` key/value heads of `x` repeated to make `h` heads, one for each query head:
head i of the result is head i // (h / g) of `x`, so each key/value head serves h / g consecutive
query heads. An `h` that is not a multiple of `g`, or an `x` with no heads, is a build error.
values.type: Tensor.Dim h -> Tensor.Tensor k d (Tensor.R3 g t j) -> Tensor.Tensor k d (Tensor.R3 h t j)

values.name: timestepEmbedding
values.comment:
Returns sinusoidal embeddings of the timesteps `t`, one row of `e` features per timestep: the
sines of the timestep times each of e / 2 frequencies, followed by their cosines, or the cosines
first when `cosFirst` is True.

Frequency k, for k = 0 … e/2 − 1, is exp(−ln(`maxPeriod`) · k / (e/2 − `shift`)). An odd `e` is a
build error. The frequencies become constants of `t`'s dtype, and the products, sines and cosines
are computed in that dtype.
values.type: { maxPeriod : Basics.Float, cosFirst : Basics.Bool, shift : Basics.Float } -> Tensor.Dim e -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R1 n) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n e)

values.name: upsampleNearest2d
values.comment:
Returns the image `x` enlarged `f` times in height and width by repeating pixels: each pixel
becomes an `f` × `f` block of copies of itself. `h2` and `w2` are the result's height and width. An
`f` below 1, or an `h2` or `w2` other than `f` times the input's, is a build error.
values.type: Basics.Int -> Tensor.Dim h2 -> Tensor.Dim w2 -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h w c) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h2 w2 c)

name: Nn.Attention
comment:
`Nn.attention` computes attention from queries, keys and values that are already split into
heads, and holds no parameters. An attention layer adds the parameters around it, and this module
provides three such layers: for each, the record of its parameters, descriptions of that record
(`Param.Spec` values) and the functions that apply it.

A layer reads a sequence `x` of `s` positions, each a row of `m` features (the _model width_), and
returns a sequence of the same shape, which `selfCached` pairs with the updated cache. Its
parameters are those of four dense layers (`Nn.Linear`). The _query_, _key_ and _value_ projections
map rows of features to queries, keys and values, and the _output_ projection maps the attention's
result back to rows of `m` features.

Between the projections and the attention, each row of a projection's output is split into _heads_:
its features are read as `h` heads of `j` features each, the first `j` features making the first
head, and each head attends separately. The heads' results are then joined back into one row each
before the output projection. Splitting and joining are reshapes, so a projection whose width is not
its number of heads times `j`, or a model width that is not h × j, is a build error when the layer
is applied, as `Tensor.factorLast3` and `Tensor.mergeLast3` describe. Their exception means here
that a split or join of a sequence with no positions accepts any sizes: `x`, or, for the keys and
values of `cross` and `attendTo`, the memory. The sizes used for this are read from the record's
`heads`, `headDim` and `model` fields (and, in `Grouped`, `kvHeads`), which a description from this
module holds as `Param.config` fields.

The three layers differ in where the keys and values come from and how many heads they have.

  - `Attention` is multi-head attention, with `h` heads for queries, keys and values alike. `self`
    projects all three from `x`. `cross` projects the keys and values from a second sequence, the
    _memory_, of the same width `m` and any length `t`.
  - `Grouped` is _grouped-query attention_: the queries have `h` heads and the keys and values
    `g`, and each key/value head serves a group of h / g query heads. Its key and value
    projections map to g × j features rather than `m`. Its queries and keys can be rotated by
    position (`Nn.Rotary`), and `selfCached` lets new positions attend to themselves and to the
    positions before them, reading the keys and values from a key/value cache (`Nn.KvCache`) into
    which it first writes their own.
  - `Cross` attends from a sequence of width `m` to a memory of another width `c`.

A description chooses which projections have a bias. `params` gives all four a trainable bias.
`paramsWith`, `groupedParams` and `crossParams` take two switches: `projectionBias` for the query,
key and value projections together, and `outBias` for the output projection. A projection without
a bias has a constant zero bias, as `Nn.Linear.paramsWithoutBias` describes.

The functions take the sequence last, so that `x |> self { causal = True } layer` reads left to
right.

aliases.name: Attention
aliases.comment:
The parameters of a multi-head attention layer of model width `m`, with `h` heads of `j`
features, in dtype `d`.

The four projections each map `m` features to `m`; `out` is the output projection. `model`,
`heads` and `headDim` hold `m`, `h` and `j`, and `self` and `cross` split and join the heads by
these sizes, not by the projections' own.
aliases.type: { query : Nn.Linear.Linear d m m, key : Nn.Linear.Linear d m m, value : Nn.Linear.Linear d m m, out : Nn.Linear.Linear d m m, model : Tensor.Dim m, heads : Tensor.Dim h, headDim : Tensor.Dim j }

aliases.name: Cross
aliases.comment:
The parameters of a cross-attention layer from a sequence of width `m` to a memory of width
`c`, in dtype `d`, with `h` heads of `j` features.

The query and output projections map `m` features to `m`, and the key and value projections map
the memory's `c` features to `m`, so that its keys and values are split into heads as the queries
are.
aliases.type: { query : Nn.Linear.Linear d m m, key : Nn.Linear.Linear d c m, value : Nn.Linear.Linear d c m, out : Nn.Linear.Linear d m m, model : Tensor.Dim m, heads : Tensor.Dim h, headDim : Tensor.Dim j }

aliases.name: Grouped
aliases.comment:
The parameters of a grouped-query attention layer of model width `m`, in dtype `d`, with `h`
query heads and `g` key/value heads, all of `j` features.

The query and output projections map `m` features to `m`, and the key and value projections map
`m` to `kv`, which is to be g × j. Each key/value head is repeated for h / g query heads, as
`Nn.repeatHeads` describes, so an `h` that is not a multiple of `g` is a build error when the layer
is applied, and with `g` equal to `h` this is the attention of `Attention`. The heads are split and
joined by `heads`, `kvHeads`, `headDim` and `model`. Nothing here reads `kvWidth`: a key or value
projection whose width is not g × j is a build error where it is split into heads, unless `x` has
no positions, as `Tensor.factorLast3` describes, whatever `kvWidth` holds.
aliases.type: { query : Nn.Linear.Linear d m m, key : Nn.Linear.Linear d m kv, value : Nn.Linear.Linear d m kv, out : Nn.Linear.Linear d m m, model : Tensor.Dim m, kvWidth : Tensor.Dim kv, heads : Tensor.Dim h, kvHeads : Tensor.Dim g, headDim : Tensor.Dim j }

values.name: attendTo
values.comment:
Returns the attention of the sequence `x` to `memory`, a sequence of `t` positions of `c`
features: as `cross` does, with the keys and values projected from `c` features to `m`. Every
position of `x` attends to every position of `memory`.
values.type: Nn.Attention.Cross d m c h j -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 t c) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s m) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s m)

values.name: cross
values.comment:
Returns the attention of the sequence `x` to `memory`, a sequence of `t` positions of `m`
features: the queries are projected from `x`, the keys and values from `memory`, and every position
of `x` attends to every position of `memory`. The result is projected back as in `self`.
values.type: Nn.Attention.Attention d m h j -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 t m) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s m) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s m)

values.name: crossParams
values.comment:
Returns the description of a `Cross` layer, with its biases chosen as in `paramsWith`.

Its tensor fields are those of `query`, `key`, `value` and `out`, in that order, and `model`,
`heads` and `headDim` are config fields holding `m`, `h` and `j`.
values.type: Tensor.DType Basics.Float d -> { projectionBias : Basics.Bool, outBias : Basics.Bool } -> Tensor.Dim m -> Tensor.Dim c -> Tensor.Dim h -> Tensor.Dim j -> Param.Spec (Nn.Attention.Cross d m c h j)

values.name: groupedParams
values.comment:
Returns the description of a `Grouped` layer, with its biases chosen as in `paramsWith`.

Its tensor fields are those of `query`, `key`, `value` and `out`, in that order, and `model`,
`kvWidth`, `heads`, `kvHeads` and `headDim` are config fields holding `m`, `kv`, `h`, `g` and `j`.
values.type: Tensor.DType Basics.Float d -> { projectionBias : Basics.Bool, outBias : Basics.Bool } -> Tensor.Dim m -> Tensor.Dim kv -> Tensor.Dim h -> Tensor.Dim g -> Tensor.Dim j -> Param.Spec (Nn.Attention.Grouped d m kv h g j)

values.name: params
values.comment:
Returns the description of an `Attention` layer of width `m` with `h` heads of `j` features,
each projection described by `Nn.Linear.params`, so with a trainable weight and a trainable bias.

Its tensor fields are those of `query`, `key`, `value` and `out`, in that order, and `model`,
`heads` and `headDim` are config fields holding `m`, `h` and `j`.
values.type: Tensor.DType Basics.Float d -> Tensor.Dim m -> Tensor.Dim h -> Tensor.Dim j -> Param.Spec (Nn.Attention.Attention d m h j)

values.name: paramsWith
values.comment:
Returns the description of an `Attention` layer as `params` does, except that the biases are
chosen: when `projectionBias` is True the query, key and value projections have a trainable bias,
and when `outBias` is True the output projection has one. A projection without one has a constant
zero bias, as `Nn.Linear.paramsWithoutBias` describes. With both True this is the description
`params` returns.
values.type: Tensor.DType Basics.Float d -> { projectionBias : Basics.Bool, outBias : Basics.Bool } -> Tensor.Dim m -> Tensor.Dim h -> Tensor.Dim j -> Param.Spec (Nn.Attention.Attention d m h j)

values.name: self
values.comment:
Returns the self-attention of the sequence `x`: its queries, keys and values are all
projected from `x`, the heads attend as `Nn.attention` describes, and the result is their output
projected back to rows of `m` features.

With `causal` True, position i attends only to positions 0 … i, as `Nn.causalAttention`
describes. With it False, every position attends to every position.
values.type: { causal : Basics.Bool } -> Nn.Attention.Attention d m h j -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s m) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s m)

values.name: selfCached
values.comment:
Returns `cache` with the keys and values of `x` written into it, together with the
grouped-query self-attention of `x`, its `s` positions attending to the cache's.

Position i of `x` is taken to be position p + i of the sequence, where p is the value of
`position`. The keys and values of `x` are written into the cache at positions p … p + s − 1, as
`Nn.KvCache.write` describes; with `rotary`, the queries and keys are first rotated for those
position values, so the keys written are the rotated ones. Position p + i then attends to the
cache's positions 0 … p + i, whatever the cache holds there, through the mask `Nn.causalMaskAt`
makes. There is no `causal` switch.

A written position outside the cache's 0 … t − 1 is not a build error; `Tensor.Eval` refuses the
write when it runs, as `Nn.KvCache.write` says.
values.type: { rotary : Maybe.Maybe Nn.Rotary.Rotary } -> Nn.Attention.Grouped d m kv h g j -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Int Tensor.I64 Tensor.R0 -> Nn.KvCache.Cache d g t j -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s m) -> ( Nn.KvCache.Cache d g t j, Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s m) )

values.name: selfGrouped
values.comment:
Returns the grouped-query self-attention of the sequence `x`: as `self` does, except that the
keys and values are split into `g` heads and each is repeated for its group of query heads.

When `rotary` holds a `Rotary` and a positions tensor, the queries and keys are rotated as
`Nn.Rotary.apply` describes, position i of `x` being rotated for the value at index i of the
positions tensor. The values are not rotated. `causal` is as in `self`.
values.type: { causal : Basics.Bool, rotary : Maybe.Maybe ( Nn.Rotary.Rotary, Tensor.Tensor Basics.Int Tensor.I64 (Tensor.R1 s) ) } -> Nn.Attention.Grouped d m kv h g j -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s m) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 s m)

name: Nn.Conv2d
comment:
A 2-D convolution layer slides a small filter over an image and, at each position it stops at,
mixes the channels under the filter into new channels. This module provides that layer and its
transpose.

Images are NHWC: rank-4 tensors of (batch, height, width, channels). A filter is a rank-4 tensor of
(kernel height, kernel width, input channels, output channels), the layout MAX calls RSCF, where the
input and output channels are those of `apply`. A filter in another layout, such as PyTorch's OIHW
(output channels, input channels, kernel height, kernel width), must be permuted before it can be a
`Conv2d`'s. The kernel's two axes carry this module's tags, `KernelH` and `KernelW`.

The height and width of a convolution's result follow from the input's, the kernel's, the strides
and the padding, and no rank type can compute them. `apply` and `applyTransposed` therefore take
the result's height and width as `Dim`s, whose tags name the result's axes in its type, and compare
their sizes with the computed ones when the tensor is made, unless the result has already failed for
another reason. A mismatch is a build error, as `Tensor` describes; so is an input whose channels
differ in size from those the filter takes. `applySame` takes no `Dim`s, because its result has the
input's height and width.

Strides and padding are the only settings: there is no dilation.

unions.name: KernelH
unions.comment:
The axis tag of a filter's first axis, the kernel's height.

Its constructor is not exposed, so a `Dim KernelH` comes from `kernel`.

unions.name: KernelW
unions.comment:
The axis tag of a filter's second axis, the kernel's width.

Its constructor is not exposed, so a `Dim KernelW` comes from `kernel`.

aliases.name: Conv2d
aliases.comment:
The parameters of a convolution layer, which `apply` uses to map `c` channels to `o`: a
`filter` of shape (kernel height, kernel width, `c`, `o`) and a `bias` with one value per output
channel.

`applyTransposed` does not read `bias`.
aliases.type: { filter : Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 Nn.Conv2d.KernelH Nn.Conv2d.KernelW c o), bias : Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R1 o) }

aliases.name: Padding
aliases.comment:
The rows of padding above and below an image and the columns to its left and right.

`apply` pads its input with them; `applyTransposed` removes them from its result.
aliases.type: { top : Basics.Int, bottom : Basics.Int, left : Basics.Int, right : Basics.Int }

values.name: apply
values.comment:
Applies the layer `p` to the NHWC input `x` with the given `stride` (rows, columns) and
`padding`, adding the bias to every output channel, and declares the result's height and width to
be the sizes of `h2` and `w2`.

For an input of height h and width w, a kernel of kh × kw and strides (sh, sw), the result has
(h + top + bottom − kh) // sh + 1 rows and (w + left + right − kw) // sw + 1 columns, where `//` is
Elm's integer division, which rounds toward zero. A result with fewer than one row or column is a
build error. So, unless the result has already failed, is an `h2` or `w2` whose size differs from
the computed one.
values.type: { stride : ( Basics.Int, Basics.Int ), padding : Nn.Conv2d.Padding } -> Tensor.Dim h2 -> Tensor.Dim w2 -> Nn.Conv2d.Conv2d d c o -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h w c) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h2 w2 o)

values.name: applySame
values.comment:
Applies the layer `p` to `x` with stride 1 and the padding that keeps the input's height and
width: (k − 1) / 2 rows or columns on each side for a kernel side of k. The bias is added to every
output channel.

The kernel's height and width must both be odd; an even one is a build error.
values.type: Nn.Conv2d.Conv2d d c o -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h w c) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h w o)

values.name: applyTransposed
values.comment:
Applies the transposed convolution of `p`'s filter to `x`, with the given `stride` and
`padding`, and declares the result's height and width to be the sizes of `h2` and `w2`. The bias of
`p` is not used.

This is the transpose of the convolution `apply` makes with the same filter, strides and padding,
leaving out the bias. A `Conv2d d o c`, which `apply` uses to map `o` channels to `c`, here maps `c`
channels to `o`, and the padding is removed from the result instead of added to the input.

For an input of height h and width w, a kernel of kh × kw and strides (sh, sw), the result has
(h − 1) · sh + kh − top − bottom rows and (w − 1) · sw + kw − left − right columns. Unless the
result has already failed, an `h2` or `w2` whose size differs from the computed one is a build
error. Unlike in `apply`, a computed size of zero or less is not a build error in itself.
values.type: { stride : ( Basics.Int, Basics.Int ), padding : Nn.Conv2d.Padding } -> Tensor.Dim h2 -> Tensor.Dim w2 -> Nn.Conv2d.Conv2d d o c -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h w c) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R4 n h2 w2 o)

values.name: kernel
values.comment:
Returns the kernel height and width `( kh, kw )` as dimensions with this module's tags, for
writing a filter's shape outside `params`: for example the shape of a filter in PyTorch's
(output, input, kh, kw) layout, before it is permuted into a `Conv2d`'s.
values.type: ( Basics.Int, Basics.Int ) -> ( Tensor.Dim Nn.Conv2d.KernelH, Tensor.Dim Nn.Conv2d.KernelW )

values.name: params
values.comment:
Describes a `Conv2d` from `c` channels to `o` with a `kh × kw` kernel, given as
`kernel = ( kh, kw )`. It has two trainable fields: first the filter, drawn as `Param.heUniform`
describes for the shape (kh, kw, `c`, `o`), and then the bias, all zeros.
values.type: Tensor.DType Basics.Float d -> { kernel : ( Basics.Int, Basics.Int ) } -> Tensor.Dim c -> Tensor.Dim o -> Param.Spec (Nn.Conv2d.Conv2d d c o)

name: Nn.Embedding
comment:
A model whose inputs are tokens, integer ids drawn from a vocabulary, needs a vector for each
token to compute with. This module describes the table as a parameter record and gives two functions
over it.

The vocabulary has `v` entries, and a token is named by its _id_, an integer from 0 to v − 1. The
_table_ is a `v` × `m` matrix whose row i is the vector of `m` features for the token with id i.
`apply` looks rows up by id, turning a sequence of ids into a sequence of vectors. `unembed` goes
the other way: it scores a vector against every row, giving one score for each entry of the
vocabulary.

Using the input table for that output scoring, rather than a separate output matrix, is called
_tying_ the two. A model that uses both functions on one `Embedding` has a single table that
serves both.

name: Nn.FeedForward
comment:
A feed-forward block takes rows of `m` features to rows of `f` hidden features and back to `m`.
This module provides the _gated_ form of that block, with its activation as an argument.

The block is three dense layers (`Nn.Linear`). The _gate_ and _up_ projections each map `m`
features to `f`, and the _down_ projection maps `f` back to `m`. In the gated form the hidden row is
the element-wise product of two projections of the input: the gate projection passed through the
activation, and the up projection as it is. For input x and activation `act`, the block is

    down (act (gate x) · up x)

where · multiplies element by element. With `Tensor.silu` as the activation this is the variant
called SwiGLU, and with `Tensor.gelu` the one called GEGLU, using the erf form of GELU;
`Tensor.geluTanh` gives GEGLU with the tanh approximation instead.

name: Nn.GroupNorm
comment:
Group normalisation of images: each image is normalised by statistics of its own, taken over
groups of its channels, and never by statistics of the other images in its batch, so one image's
result does not depend on the rest of the batch.

Images here are NHWC: rank-4 tensors of (images, height, width, channels). The `c` channels are
split into `groups` _groups_ of `c / groups` consecutive channels, in their order on the last axis:
group `g` holds channels `g * c / groups` up to, but not including, `(g + 1) * c / groups`. Within
one image, each group is normalised over all of its positions and all of its channels together:
its mean is subtracted, and the difference is multiplied by `1 / sqrt (variance + epsilon)`, where
the variance is the mean of the squared differences (divided by the number of elements, not by one
less). Each channel is then multiplied by its own `scale` and shifted by its own `bias`.

For an `f16` or `bf16` image, the normalisation is computed in `f32` and its result cast back to the
image's dtype; the scale and bias are then applied in the image's dtype.

name: Nn.KvCache
comment:
Attention reads the keys and values of every position it attends to. When a sequence is
generated a few positions at a time, the keys and values of the earlier positions can be kept
instead of being computed again at each step, and a key/value cache is where they are kept. This
module is that cache: the record that holds it, its signature, and the write that replaces some
of its positions.

A cache has a fixed size. It holds `t` positions, for `g` heads of `j` features each: its keys and
its values both have shape g × t × j, with the positions on axis 1. A write replaces `s`
consecutive positions, from a given one, with the keys and values of `s` new positions, and leaves
the size as it was.

The cache does not record how many of its positions have been written. The position a write starts
at is an argument of `write`, and the cache's tensors hold all `t` positions, those not yet written
included.

aliases.comment:
A key/value cache of dtype `d`: the keys and the values held for each of `t` positions, for `g`
heads of `j` features each.
aliases.type: { keys : Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R3 g t j), values : Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R3 g t j) }

values.name: sig
values.comment:
Creates the signature of a cache of dtype `dt` and sizes `g`, `t` and `j`: two tensors, the keys
then the values, labelled `keys` and `values`.

Both slots are fed, like those of any `Signature` leaf. Keeping the cache in buffers between runs is
up to whatever builds the graph: `Infer.step` makes the slots of its state signature resident.
values.type: Tensor.DType Basics.Float d -> Tensor.Dim g -> Tensor.Dim t -> Tensor.Dim j -> Signature.Sig (Nn.KvCache.Cache d g t j)

values.name: write
values.comment:
Returns the cache with the keys (the second argument) and the values (the third) of `s` new
positions written at positions p … p + s − 1 along its positions axis, where p is the value of the
first argument. The keys replace the cache's keys there and the values its values; the other
positions are unchanged.

`s` is read from the keys. Values for a different number of positions make the new values a build
error. A written position outside 0 … t − 1 is not a build error; `Tensor.Eval` refuses it when it
runs, as for `Tensor.put`.

name: Nn.LayerNorm
comment:
Layer normalisation as a layer with learnt parameters: the parameter record, its description
for `Param`, and the functions that apply it to a tensor whose last axis holds features.

Layer normalisation treats each lane along the last axis on its own, a lane being the `m` features
at one position. It subtracts the lane's mean and divides by √(variance + ε), where the variance is
the mean squared deviation from that mean (a division by `m`, not `m − 1`) and ε is the record's
`epsilon`. The normalised lane is then multiplied element by element by the `gain` and added to the
`bias`, two learnt vectors of length `m`. For an input lane `x` and output lane `y`:

    y = (x − mean) / √(variance + ε) · gain + bias

Each application builds one layer-normalisation primitive, given the input in its own dtype `d`:
unlike `Nn.RmsNorm`, nothing here casts an f16 or bf16 input to f32 first. The types tie the gain
and bias to the last axis's tag only, so a gain or bias whose size differs from that axis is a build
error.

`apply` and `apply3` read ε from the record. On MAX it becomes a constant of dtype `d`, so for f16
or bf16 ε is rounded to that dtype.
aliases.type: { gain : Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R1 m), bias : Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R1 m), epsilon : Basics.Float }

values.comment:

refused.

name: Nn.Linear
comment:
A dense layer maps each row of `i` input features to a row of `o` output features by the affine
map x · weight + bias. This module is that layer: the record of its parameters, two descriptions of
that record (`Param.Spec` values), and the functions that apply it.

The weight has shape (i, o): its rows index the inputs and its columns the outputs, so a row of `i`
features times the weight is a row of `o` features. A weight stored the other way round, (o, i),
has to be transposed before it can be used here.

The bias is `o` values added to every output row. `params` describes it as a trainable field and
`paramsWithoutBias` as a constant zero vector. Both descriptions describe the same record type, so a
`Linear` is applied in the same way whichever of them made it.

name: Nn.RmsNorm
comment:
Root-mean-square normalisation: a layer that divides each vector of features by its root mean
square, after adding a constant to the mean square, and multiplies each feature by a weight of its
own.

The features are the elements along the last axis of the input `x`, and each vector of them is
normalised separately:

    y = x / sqrt (mean (x²) + ε) · scale

The mean is taken over the last axis, ε is `epsilon`, and `scale` holds one weight per feature.
The types tie `scale` to the last axis's tag only, so a `scale` whose length differs from that
axis's size is a build error. Unlike `Nn.LayerNorm`, it subtracts no mean and adds no bias.

For an `f16` or `bf16` `x`, everything before the multiplication by `scale` is computed in `f32`,
and the result is cast back to `x`'s dtype before it is multiplied by `scale`. An `f32` or `f64`
`x` is computed in its own dtype throughout.

name: Nn.Rotary
comment:
Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) put a vector's position into it by rotating it, so that the
dot product of two vectors rotated this way depends on their positions only through the difference
between them, up to rounding. This module applies them to a tensor of features per head and
position.

The tensor rotated, `x`, has three axes: heads, positions and features, of sizes `h`, `s` and `j`.
Each head's `j` features at one position are taken as `j / 2` pairs, and each pair `(a, b)` is
rotated as a point in the plane, becoming `(a cos θ − b sin θ, a sin θ + b cos θ)`. For pair `k`
at index `i` of the positions axis the angle is `θ = p · base^(−2k/j)` radians, where `p` is the
integer the positions tensor (below) holds at `i` and `base` is the field of that name in `Rotary`:
pair 0 turns by one radian per unit of `p`, and each later pair turns more slowly when `base` is
greater than 1. A `j` that is odd is a build error.

Which two features make up pair `k` is the _pairing_. There are two conventions, given by
`Pairing`, and they differ only in the order of the features.

The positions are a tensor of `s` integers, one for each index of the positions axis of `x`, so
they need not be known when the graph is built: they can be computed in the graph or given as an
input with each run. The positions axis of `x` and the axis of the positions tensor have one tag,
so a positions tensor whose axis has another tag is a compile error, and one of another size is a
build error.

The angles, and their cosines and sines, have the dtype `f32` whatever the dtype of `x`. The
cosines and sines are then cast to the dtype of `x`, and the rotation is computed in it.

unions.name: Pairing
unions.comment:
Which two of a head's `j` features are rotated together as pair `k`.

With `Interleaved`, pair `k` is features `2k` and `2k + 1`, two neighbours.

With `Halves`, pair `k` is features `k` and `k + j/2`, one from each half of the features.

In both, the first feature of the pair is the `a` of the rotation and the second the `b`, and pair
`k` turns at the same rate. So applying `Halves` gives the same values as reordering the features
so that each pair is adjacent, applying `Interleaved`, and putting the features back in their
order. Which of the two is right for `x` therefore depends only on how its features are ordered.

aliases.name: Rotary
aliases.comment:
The settings of a rotary embedding: how fast its angles turn, and how features are paired.

`base` sets the rates: pair `k` of `j` features turns by `base^(−2k/j)` radians per unit of the
position value `p`.
Nothing checks it.

values.comment:
Returns `x` with the features of every head at index `i` of the positions axis rotated for the
position value `positions[i]`, pair by pair, with the rates and pairing of `r`.

The angles, cosines and sines are computed in `f32`; the cosines and sines are then cast to the
dtype of `x`, in which the rotation is computed. An odd number of features, or a `positions` whose
size is not that of the positions axis of `x`, is a build error.

name: Nn.Sampling
comment:
Producing a sequence one token at a time means choosing each next token from a row of scores
over a vocabulary, and this module makes that choice inside the graph.

The scores are a matrix of _logits_, one row per sequence and one column per token of the
vocabulary. A row's logits are unnormalised log-probabilities: the row's softmax is the
probability of each token coming next. A _token_ is a column's position in its row, and every
function here that chooses gives one `int64` position per row.

A choice is either the most likely token (`greedy`) or a token drawn at random from the row's
probabilities (`sample`). A draw can first be confined to the likeliest tokens of the row: those
whose logits are at or above the row's `k`-th largest (_top-k_, `keepTopK`), or the _nucleus_
(_top-p_, `nucleus`), which is the smallest set of most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to
at least a given total, and the whole row when its probabilities add up to less.

Confining a draw does not shorten a row. Each logit left out is replaced by a large negative value,
far below any ordinary logit, so that it keeps no meaningful probability. That value is the lowest
finite value of `f16`, `f32` or `f64` for those dtypes. For `bf16` it is the lowest finite `f32`
value, which is outside `bf16`'s range.

There is no temperature parameter. Dividing the logits by a temperature first draws at that
temperature. The draws are made by `Tensor.Random.categorical`, whose module says what one seed
gives and when two draws need different seeds.

@docs greedy, sample


# Top-k and top-p

`keepTopK` returns logits; `nucleus` filters and draws in one step.

@docs keepTopK, nucleus

values.name: greedy
values.comment:
Returns, for each row of the logits, the position of its most likely token, the one with the
largest logit.
values.type: Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n v) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Int Tensor.I64 (Tensor.R1 n)

values.name: keepTopK
values.comment:
Returns `logits` with every logit of a row replaced by the large negative value the module
description gives, except those at or above the row's `k`-th largest.

A logit equal to the `k`-th largest is kept, so a row with ties at the `k`-th place keeps more than
`k` logits. A `k` below 1 or above the number of tokens is a build error, as for `Tensor.topK`.
values.type: Basics.Int -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n v) -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n v)

values.name: nucleus
values.comment:
Returns, for each row of `logits`, a token drawn with `seed` from the row with the tokens
outside its nucleus replaced.

A token is in the nucleus when the probabilities of the tokens ranked above it, most likely first,
add up to less than `p`. The draw is made as `sample` makes it, on the row sorted most likely first
with every token outside the nucleus replaced as `keepTopK` replaces them, and the position drawn
is mapped back to the token's position in the row. Because the draw is on the sorted row, one seed
need not give the token `sample` gives, even when the nucleus holds the whole row.

A `p` of 0 or less leaves the nucleus empty: every logit of the row is replaced by the same value,
so the result is not a draw from the row's probabilities.
values.type: Basics.Float -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n v) -> Tensor.Random.Seed -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Int Tensor.I64 (Tensor.R1 n)

values.name: sample
values.comment:
Returns, for each row of the logits, a token drawn with the seed, with the row's softmax as
its probabilities. It is `Tensor.Random.categorical`.
values.type: Tensor.Tensor Basics.Float d (Tensor.R2 n v) -> Tensor.Random.Seed -> Tensor.Tensor Basics.Int Tensor.I64 (Tensor.R1 n)

name: Nn.Stack
comment:
A multilayer perceptron has hidden layers whose widths matter only inside it, and this module
describes one without giving each hidden width an axis tag of its own.

A _dense layer_ maps each row x of its input to x · W + b and then applies its _activation_ to each
element, W being a weight of input width × output width and b a bias of output width. A _stack_ is
dense layers applied one after another, each layer's input width being the output width of the
layer before it.

A description of a stack (`Seq i o`) lists its layers, each with its output width and its
activation, and is written as a pipeline:

    mlp =
        Nn.Stack.input
            |> Nn.Stack.dense 512 Nn.Stack.relu
            |> Nn.Stack.dense 256 Nn.Stack.relu
            |> Nn.Stack.denseTo classes Nn.Stack.none

Only the two ends of a stack are tagged. `i` is the tag of its input features and `o` the tag of
its last layer's outputs. A _hidden width_ is the width of a layer that is not the last, and `dense`
gives one without a tag: it takes the layer's width as a plain `Int`, and when it adds the last
layer the stack's `o` is `Width` instead of a tag the program declares. `denseTo` takes a `Dim`, and its outputs carry that
`Dim`'s tag. When the stack is applied, the first layer's product compares the inputs' width with
that layer's weight.

`params` turns a description, a dtype and the input width into a `Param.Spec` of the weights and
biases, and `apply` and `applyWithDropout` apply the stack those parameters make.
